title: Platform engineering and your capstone
intro: Part 19 is the last part. Day 67 shows what happens when many teams need what you built: platform teams turn it into golden paths, and FinOps gives every cost an owner. Day 68 is your capstone. One change travels through every part of the course with a check at each stage, and you finish with a plan for what to learn next.

lessons.title: Platform engineering and FinOps
lessons.goal: By the end you can explain what a platform team builds and how to tell if it works, turn hello-devops into a golden path template, and make cluster cost visible per team.

guess.q: A company installs Backstage, a developer portal. Six months later, few teams use it. What is the most likely cause?
options: Backstage is too slow for large companies
The portal had little real self-service behind it
Developers need a Backstage certificate first
A portal only works after a move to Kubernetes
guess.why: A portal is only the front door. Teams adopt a platform when it lets them do real work faster, such as creating a service with CI and deploys already wired up.

terms.plain: Building and running internal tools and services so product teams can ship by themselves.
The self-service capabilities a platform team offers, such as templates, pipelines, environments and dashboards.
A supported, ready-made way to do a common task, such as creating a new service, that is easier than doing it alone.
A web front door to the platform with a service catalog, templates and docs. Backstage is the best-known one.
The practice of making cloud cost visible and shared between engineering, finance and the business.
Giving every cost an owner, usually with tags in the cloud and labels in Kubernetes.
A report that shows each team the cost of what it used, while the money stays in a central budget.
What you pay for capacity that no workload requested, such as empty space on nodes.

sections.body:
List what hello-devops needs by now. A Dockerfile, two workflows with pinned actions, Kubernetes YAML and an Argo CD Application. A ServiceMonitor, a dashboard, log shipping and tracing. Policies, and a way to get secrets. You learned all of it in this course. Now picture 40 product teams, each building that alone. They solve the same problems 40 times, in 40 slightly different ways, and whoever is on call has to learn every one.

Most large companies answer this with platform engineering. A platform team builds an internal developer platform (IDP): the self-service capabilities that product teams use to build, ship and run software. The [CNCF platforms white paper](https://tag-app-delivery.cncf.io/whitepapers/platforms/) puts self-service at the centre. A developer gets an environment, a database or a pipeline without filing a ticket and waiting a week.

The team runs the platform as a product, with developers as its customers. In practice, a platform team:
- Talks to its users and watches where they get stuck.
- Publishes a roadmap and takes feature requests.
- Measures success by adoption and speed, never by the number of tools installed.

A classic operations team does work for other teams, through tickets. A platform team builds things so that other teams can do the work themselves. DevOps ideas such as shared ownership and automation still apply; the platform makes them the easy option.

refs.title: Platform engineering in the 2025 DORA report (DORA community discussion)

sections.body:
The platform's main product is the golden path, which some companies call the paved road. It is a supported, ready-made way to do a common job. "Create a new service" is the classic one. You fill in a name and a team. You get a repository with a Dockerfile, CI, a release workflow, Kubernetes YAML, an Argo CD Application and a dashboard, already wired together.

The [CNCF maturity model](https://github.com/cncf/tag-app-delivery/blob/main/platforms-maturity-model/v1/index.md) describes golden paths as documentation and templates built on compliant and tested patterns. Each of those two words is a promise:
- Compliant: security and policy are built in, so the easy way is also the safe way.
- Tested: the platform team keeps the template working, so a new service starts with current versions.

Teams may still leave the path when they have a good reason. If many teams leave it, the path is wrong, and that is the most useful feedback a platform team gets.

Developers find these paths through a developer portal. Backstage, created at Spotify and now a CNCF incubating project, is the best-known framework for building one. It has:
- A software catalog: every service, its owner, its docs and what it depends on.
- Software templates: golden paths you start from a form.
- TechDocs: documentation written in Markdown next to the code.
- Plugins that show CI runs, Kubernetes state, costs and more on each service's page.

Backstage is the shop front. The platform is the shop behind it: the templates, pipelines and clusters. With one repository and one team you do not need a portal at all; a GitHub template repository does the job.

sections.h: Is the platform working? Maturity and developer experience
sections.body:
The [CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model](https://github.com/cncf/tag-app-delivery/blob/main/platforms-maturity-model/v1/index.md) lets a team check where it stands. It scores five aspects, each on four levels: provisional, operational, scalable and optimizing.
- Investment: from volunteers, to a dedicated team, to a product, to an enabled ecosystem.
- Adoption: from erratic, to pushed by mandate, to pulled by teams who want it, to teams who contribute.
- Interfaces: from custom processes, to standard tools, to self-service, to integrated services.
- Operations: from by request, to centrally tracked, to centrally enabled, to managed services.
- Measurement: from ad hoc, to consistent collection, to insights, to numbers plus user feedback.

Score each aspect on its own. You do not need level 4 everywhere, and a CNCF blog post from September 2026 notes that many teams stall at level 2 for interfaces.

Start with the adoption row, which says the most about whether the platform helps. A platform that teams use because a manager said so sits at level 2. One that teams choose because it is faster sits at level 3.

Developer experience (DevEx) is how it feels to ship software in a company. Measure it with a few plain numbers:
- Time from "new service" to its first production deploy.
- How often a developer waits for another team.
- The DORA metrics from Day 1, for teams on the golden path and off it.

Then ask the developers directly, every quarter. At the lowest level of the model, users believe their feedback is not considered, so asking and acting on the answers already moves you up.

refs.title: Building a platform maturity model (Abby Bangser)

sections.h: FinOps: every cost gets an owner
sections.body:
In the cloud, any engineer can spend money with one command, and the bill arrives a month later with no names on it. FinOps is the practice of making that cost visible and shared between engineering, finance and the business. The FinOps Foundation, a Linux Foundation project, maintains the [framework](https://www.finops.org/framework/lifecycle/) most teams follow. It loops through three phases, again and again:
1. Inform: see who spends what, and give every cost an owner.
2. Optimize: get the same result for less, through better rates and less waste.
3. Operate: make it routine, with budgets, reviews and alerts.

Everything starts with allocation. Until a cost has an owner, every saving is a guess. In the cloud that means tags (Day 12). In Kubernetes it means labels, because many teams share one cluster. A cost tool adds up each Pod's CPU and memory requests and splits the price of the nodes by label. The lab's `policy/require-team-label.yaml` audits that every workload in hello carries a `team` label.

Then the usual levers, roughly from easy to hard:
- Right-size requests from real usage (Day 43). The scheduler reserves what you request, used or not.
- Autoscale Pods and nodes, so quiet hours cost less.
- Turn off what nobody uses: dev environments at night, forgotten test clusters.
- Commit to reserved capacity for steady load, and use spot capacity for work that can restart.

The framework now reaches beyond public cloud, through "scopes" grouped under the name Cloud+. My advice for any team: put cost on a dashboard next to latency and errors, and look at it every week.

refs.title: Microsoft Learn: the FinOps framework explained

sections.h: Showback, idle cost and cost per request
sections.body:
Once every cost has an owner, you can show each team its bill. The FinOps Foundation separates two ways to do that:
- Showback: each team gets a report of what it used, and the money stays in a central budget.
- Chargeback: the cost moves into each team's own budget in the finance system.

The framework calls showback something every FinOps practice needs, and chargeback a choice that depends on how the company does its accounting. Start with showback. Teams change what they run once they see the numbers next to their own name.

In Kubernetes the report needs one more line: idle cost. A node costs the same whether its Pods request 10% of it or 90%. Capacity that nobody requested still appears on the bill. A tool such as OpenCost, a CNCF project, splits the price of each node by the CPU, memory and GPU each workload requests, and shows what is left as idle. Give that line an owner too, usually the platform team, or every team argues about it.

Totals grow when the business grows, so they make poor targets. A unit cost works better: cost per request served, per customer, or per build. If traffic doubles and the bill grows by 40%, each request got cheaper, even though the bill went up. hello-devops already has both inputs. Prometheus counts requests in `hello_requests_total` (Day 50), and the `team` label says whose cost it is. Divide one by the other each month, and you have a number a product manager can read.

refs.title: FinOps Foundation: invoicing and chargeback (showback and chargeback)

sections.h: Guardrails belong on the golden path
sections.body:
A golden path is easy to follow because the platform team already made the hard choices. Security and policy belong in that set, built in from the start. For hello-devops, a new service made from the template starts with:
- pinned actions and least-privilege `permissions:` in every workflow (Days 27 and 63)
- a signed image with an SBOM, built by the release workflow
- its own ServiceAccount with no token mounted, and Pods that pass the restricted standard (Day 64)
- the Kyverno policies, including the `team` label that FinOps needs
- a dashboard and alerts for its own metrics

The cluster enforces the same rules for everyone, so a team that leaves the path still meets them. Roll policies out in Audit mode first, then Deny, as on Day 64. Budgets work the same way: the platform sends the cost alert, and the owning team receives it.

AI coding agents are one more kind of user of the path, and Days 65 and 66 cover how to use them and fence them in. For a platform team they change one thing. An agent follows AGENTS.md and the template's checks as literally as CI does, so a good template produces good agent changes, and a messy one produces mess faster.

sections.h: Other trends worth a line each
sections.body:
You will meet these names in job ads and conference talks:
- eBPF runs small, checked programs inside the Linux kernel. [Cilium](https://github.com/cilium/cilium) uses it for Kubernetes networking, observability and security, and can replace kube-proxy.
- [OpenTofu](https://github.com/opentofu/opentofu) is the open source fork of Terraform (Part 8). The commands are nearly the same: `tofu plan` instead of `terraform plan`.
- WebAssembly (Wasm) runs small, sandboxed programs that start very fast, as plugins inside other tools or at the edge.
- Serverless containers, such as Google Cloud Run, AWS Fargate and Azure Container Apps, run your image with no servers or cluster to manage. For one small service, that is often the simplest place to run it.

lessons.analogy: A platform works like the shared services in a big office building. Every company in the building uses the same reception, mail room, network and security desk, so no tenant builds its own. A golden path is the standard office fit-out: you move in on Monday and start work on Monday. Buildings change slowly, though, and a platform has to change every month as its users do. A tenant who tears out the standard fit-out is also telling the landlord something about it.

worked.title: Turn hello-devops into a golden path template

steps.say: Mark the repository as a template. GitHub then shows a "Use this template" button, and every repository made from it starts with a copy of the files and a fresh history.

Find every file that hard-codes the service name. Each one is a line a new team must change, and the list is the first draft of your template's instructions. In the course's reference repository, the core folders alone have 27 such files.
steps.code:
$ grep -rl hello-devops k8s chart .github argocd | wc -l
27

steps.say: Add a catalog file, so a portal such as Backstage can list the service and its owner. The catalog's `owner` and the Pods' `team` label are the same promise: nothing ships without a name on it. The full file is in Files.
steps.code:
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: production
  owner: web

steps.say: Now play the new team. Create a service from the template, and clone it.
Replace the old name everywhere, then check that none is left. `sed -i ''` is the macOS form; on Linux, leave out the `''`.
steps.code:
$ grep -rl hello-devops --exclude-dir=.git . | xargs sed -i '' 's/hello-devops/payments-api/g'
$ grep -rl hello-devops --exclude-dir=.git . | wc -l
0

steps.say: Run the same checks as the original, with `ai/check.sh` from Day 65. One fails, and it is a real template bug: sed renamed the chart inside its files, but not its folder. Fix it, and then fix the template's instructions too, so the next team never meets it. (Output trimmed.)
steps.code:
$ ai/check.sh
PASS  ruff lint
PASS  ruff format
PASS  pytest
PASS  kubeconform k8s/
FAIL  helm lint
      ==> Linting chart/payments-api
      Error unable to check Chart.yaml file in chart: stat chart/payments-api/Chart.yaml: no such file or directory
$ git mv chart/hello-devops chart/payments-api
$ ai/check.sh | tail -1
8 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped

code.title: policy/require-team-label.yaml
code.src:
# Kyverno policy: every workload in namespace hello needs a "team" label on its Pods.
# Why: cost tools add up CPU and memory per label. Without an owner label,
# a cost has no owner (the FinOps "Inform" step, Day 67).
#
# Type: ValidatingPolicy (policies.kyverno.io/v1).
# Mode: Audit. Nothing is blocked; read the failures in the PolicyReport,
# add the labels, then switch to Deny if you want.
#
# Apply: kubectl apply -f policy/require-team-label.yaml
# Read:  kubectl -n hello get policyreports -o wide
apiVersion: policies.kyverno.io/v1
kind: ValidatingPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-team-label
spec:
  validationActions:
    - Audit
  evaluation:
    background:
      enabled: true
  matchConstraints:
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        kubernetes.io/metadata.name: hello
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [pods]
      - apiGroups: [apps]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [deployments, statefulsets, daemonsets]
      - apiGroups: [batch]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [jobs, cronjobs]
  variables:
    # The labels the Pods will carry: from the Pod template of a workload,
    # or from the Pod itself.
    - name: podLabels
      expression: >-
        object.spec.?jobTemplate.?spec.?template.?metadata.?labels.orValue(
        object.spec.?template.?metadata.?labels.orValue(
        object.metadata.?labels.orValue({})))
  validations:
    - expression: >-
        'team' in variables.podLabels && variables.podLabels['team'] != ''
      message: >-
        Add a "team" label to the Pod template (spec.template.metadata.labels),
        for example team: web, so every cost has an owner.

code.title: catalog-info.yaml
code.src:
# Backstage catalog entry for this service (Day 67). Put it at the repository root.
# A developer portal reads it to list the service, its owner and its links.
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  description: The course's demo web app, with its whole delivery pipeline
  annotations:
    # Lets Backstage plugins find the repository on GitHub.
    github.com/project-slug: <your-github-user>/hello-devops
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: production
  # The owning team: the same name as the team label on the Pods.
  owner: web
code.run: git add catalog-info.yaml && git commit -m "Add a catalog entry"

commands.what: Mark a repository as a template, so new repositories can start from it.
Create a new repository from the template and clone it.
List every file that names the service.
Rename the service in every file (macOS sed; on Linux use sed -i).
Run every check in the repository, the same ones the original passes.
Audit that every workload in hello has a team label for cost allocation.
Read the policy results, including which workloads lack a team label.
Show every Pod with its team label as an extra column.

commands.cmd: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r '[.items[] | {t: (.metadata.labels.team // "no-team"), c: ([.spec.containers[].resources.requests.cpu // "0" | if endswith("m") then .[:-1]|tonumber else tonumber*1000 end] | add)}] | group_by(.t)[] | "\(.[0].t) \(map(.c)|add)m CPU"'
commands.what: Add up requested CPU per team label, in millicores.
Compare what Pods use right now with what they request (needs metrics-server).

lessons.mistake: Don't adopt every trending tool at once. Each tool in this lesson solves a problem you only feel at a certain size. Backstage pays off with many teams, not one repository, and a FinOps tool is useless until workloads carry owner labels. Get the basics solid on one real project, then add a tool when you can name the pain it removes.
lessons.real_world: The platform team's golden path gives every new service CI, signing, an Argo CD app, dashboards and a team label, all set up in one go. Finance gets a weekly cost report per team from those labels, and the teams with the biggest unused requests get a pull request that right-sizes them. When the template changes, a bot opens the same small upgrade pull request in every service, and each team reviews and merges its own.

task.title: Make cost visible per team, then score your platform
steps: Apply `policy/require-team-label.yaml` and read the PolicyReport in hello. Which workloads have no owner?
Add a `team` label to the Pod template of both Deployments, for example `team: web` for hello-devops and `team: data` for Redis. Commit, push, and let Argo CD sync.
Run the per-team CPU one-liner from Commands and write down what each team requests. Add `no-team` to your list: on kind, that is the system Pods.
Compare requests with real use from `kubectl top pods -n hello` (Day 43). Which workload reserves the most CPU it does not use?
Score your own setup on the five aspects of the CNCF maturity model, from 1 to 4. Pick one aspect and write down one change that would move it up a level.
Optional: add `catalog-info.yaml` from Files to your repository, with your own team as `owner`, and check that it matches the `team` label on your Pods.
hints: Labels on the Deployment's own metadata do not reach the Pods. Put `team` under `spec.template.metadata.labels`.
Do not add `team` to the Deployment's `selector`. The selector of an existing Deployment cannot be changed, and it does not need to be.
If `kubectl top` says metrics are not available, install metrics-server as on Day 43.
task.done_when: The PolicyReport in hello shows pass for require-team-label on both Deployments, and your one-liner prints CPU per team.

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences what a golden path is and how you would know if yours works. Mention self-service, adoption and cost.
explain_back.answer: A golden path is a supported, ready-made way to do a common job, such as creating a service with CI, signing, deploys, dashboards and policies already wired up. Developers use it by themselves, with no ticket, and the platform team keeps it current like a product. I know it works when teams choose it because it is faster, so I watch adoption, the time from new service to first deploy, and why teams leave it. Every service on the path carries an owner label, so its cost shows up per team in a showback report.

recap: Platform teams turn repeated DevOps work into self-service golden paths, run as a product for developers.
Backstage is a portal framework, the shop front; the platform is the templates, pipelines and clusters behind it.
The CNCF maturity model scores investment, adoption, interfaces, operations and measurement, each from 1 to 4.
FinOps loops through inform, optimize and operate, and starts with an owner label on every cost.
Showback comes first: each team sees its own cost, and idle cost gets its own line and an owner.
A golden path ships its guardrails: pinned actions, signed images, narrow RBAC, policies and owner labels.

check.q: Five teams each copy a different CI pipeline and Dockerfile. A new platform team wants to help. What is the best first step?
options: Ban every pipeline the platform team did not write
Ask each team to build its own Backstage plugin
Offer a golden path template teams can adopt
Move every team to a different cloud provider
check.why: A golden path makes the good way the easy way through self-service, without forcing teams onto it.

check.q: Your cluster bill doubled, and nobody knows which team caused it. Which FinOps step comes first?
options: Label every workload with its owning team
Move every workload to spot instances
Turn off all dev environments today
Rewrite the services to run serverless
check.why: Allocation comes first: until each cost has an owner, every saving is a guess.

check.q: Traffic to a service doubled this quarter, and its share of the cluster bill grew by 40%. What happened to its cost per request?
options: It rose, so the team overspent
It stayed the same, by definition
Nothing can be said without prices
It fell by about 30%
check.why: 1.4 times the cost for 2 times the requests is 0.7 times the cost per request: the bill grew, and each request got cheaper.

interview.q: What is platform engineering, and how is it different from a classic operations team?
interview.a: Platform engineering builds an internal developer platform that product teams use by themselves: templates, pipelines, environments and observability, offered as golden paths. A classic operations team often does the work for other teams through tickets. A platform team treats the platform as a product, talks to its users and measures success by adoption and by how quickly and safely teams ship. The CNCF maturity model is a useful way to check where a platform stands.

interview.q: How would you start a FinOps practice for a Kubernetes platform?
interview.a: I would start with allocation: every workload gets a team label, enforced first in Audit mode by a policy, and every cloud resource gets an owner tag. With that, a cost tool can split node costs by the CPU and memory each team requests, and finance and engineers look at the same numbers. Then I would right-size requests from real usage, add autoscaling, and turn off idle environments. Cost goes on a dashboard next to latency and errors, and teams review it every week.

interview.q: How do you keep a golden path template from going stale?
interview.a: I treat the template as a product with its own CI, so every change to it runs the checks a real service would. Dependabot keeps its pinned actions, base images and chart versions current, and template changes reach existing services as small pull requests that each team reviews. I let teams change what they need, because a path nobody can adjust gets copied once and then drifts. And I measure it: time to first deploy, how many teams use it, and why the others left.

deeper.body:
A GitHub template repository copies files, and the new team does the rest by hand, as in the worked example. A Backstage software template does more in one form. It is a YAML file of kind `Template` (apiVersion `scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3`) that asks for parameters, such as the service name and the owning team, and then runs steps:
1. `fetch:template` copies a skeleton folder and fills the parameters into it.
2. `publish:github` creates the repository and pushes the result.
3. `catalog:register` adds the new service's `catalog-info.yaml` to the catalog.

The scaffolder fills in the name only where the template's author put a placeholder. So the worked example's bug becomes a question for the author: does every place that needs the name, folder names included, have one? Test the template the way you tested the copy, by creating a service from it and running every check.

Then find out whether the path helps. The questions I would ask after three months:
- How long does it take from "new service" to the first production deploy, on the path and off it?
- How many teams use the path, and why did the others leave it?
- Do the DORA metrics from Day 1 look better for services on the path?

Watch for two failure modes. If teams cannot change anything in a template, they copy it once and drift away. And templates age: base images, action SHAs and chart versions go stale. Keep the template under CI and Dependabot, so every new service starts current, and send template changes to existing services as pull requests.

Finally, connect the path to cost. Every service the template creates gets its owner in two places: `spec.owner` in the catalog and the `team` label on its Pods. Then the showback report and the catalog agree on who owns what, and a cost spike has a team's name next to it on the first day.

lessons.title: Your capstone, and what to learn next
lessons.goal: By the end you can take hello-devops and hello-jvm through every part of the course as one capstone, prove each stage with a check, present the result, and plan your next certification and three months of learning.

guess.q: You want to show an interviewer that you can do DevOps work. Which gives the strongest evidence?
options: A list of 20 tools on your CV
A certificate from a multiple-choice exam
A repo where a commit becomes a checked deploy
A screenshot of a busy Grafana dashboard
guess.why: A working repository with checks shows you can connect the pieces and prove it. Certificates help with filters, but even the CKA curriculum gives troubleshooting the biggest weight, and projects teach that.

terms.plain: One final project that uses every part of a course together, end to end.
A runnable test that proves one piece of work is done, with a clear pass or fail.
A planned session where you break something on purpose and watch how the system and you respond.
Short written steps for one known problem: how to notice it, check it and fix it.
Architecture decision record: a short note on one technical decision, the options and why you chose one.
The official list of an exam's domains and their weights, published by the exam's owner.

sections.h: What the capstone is, and why it works
sections.body:
A capstone is one final project that uses every part of a course together. Yours has a simple story: one small code change travels from your laptop to users, and at every step you can prove it got there.

Each lesson already had a task, so why one more project? Knowledge sticks when you use it again, later and in a new mix. Each part taught one tool in a clean room. The capstone puts them all in one room, where they get in each other's way as they do at work. A Kyverno policy blocks your Argo CD sync, or a port-forward you forgot makes Prometheus look empty. You cannot practise fixing that kind of clash one tool at a time.

You work with both lab apps:
- hello-devops, the Python app you have shipped since Day 2, through the full pipeline to kind.
- hello-jvm, the Kotlin build from Part 7, built and tested by Gradle in its own CI.

Three rules keep it manageable:
1. Go in order. Each stage depends on the ones before it.
2. A stage is done when its acceptance check passes, not when it looks fine.
3. Commit after each stage, so you can always go back to the last green point.

Expect several sittings, perhaps a week or two of your usual 45 minutes a day. Nothing in it is new material, so all of that time goes into practice.

sections.h: The checklist: 14 stages, each with a check
sections.body:
Each line is one stage, the part it comes from, and the acceptance check that proves it:
1. Foundations (Parts 0 to 3): `pytest -q` and `ruff check .` pass, and you can explain every line of `curl -v localhost:8000/healthz`.
2. Containers (Part 5): `docker compose up` counts visits through Redis, and the image runs as user 10001.
3. CI (Part 6): a pull request runs `ci.yml`, a red check blocks the merge, and tag `v1.2.0` pushes an image to GHCR.
4. JVM build (Part 7): in hello-jvm, `./gradlew build` passes from a clean clone, its CI is green, and its image answers `/healthz`.
5. Infrastructure (Part 8): right after `terraform apply` in `infra/local`, `terraform plan` reports no changes.
6. Kubernetes (Part 10): the hello-devops rollout completes on kind, and `curl localhost:8081` shows visits counting up.
7. GitOps (Part 11): a merged change reaches the cluster with no kubectl, Argo CD shows Synced and Healthy, and `git revert` rolls back.
8. Metrics (Part 12): Prometheus returns a value for `sum(rate(hello_requests_total[5m]))`, and one of your Day 52 alerts fires when you break something.
9. Dashboards (Part 13): your RED dashboard, provisioned from files, shows a burst of traffic within a minute.
10. Logs (Part 14): Kibana finds hello-devops log lines from the last five minutes.
11. Traces (Part 14): Jaeger shows a trace for hello-devops, and you can name its slowest span.
12. Dynatrace (Part 16, optional): during a trial, Dynatrace shows the hello-devops service from kind, and a DQL query returns its logs.
13. Security (Part 17): `security/verify-release.sh` passes for 1.2.0, gitleaks finds nothing, and Kyverno rejects `:latest`.
14. AI and platform (Parts 18 and 19): the Day 66 agent kubeconfig can read but not delete. Every workload has a team label, and you can print CPU per team.

Stage 12 is optional because the Dynatrace trial is time-limited. Do it last, so the trial clock starts when everything else already works.

Git and Python have no stage of their own because every stage uses them. AWS, Ansible and a service mesh are optional extras here, since the capstone runs on kind. If you want them, add one stage for each:
- AWS (Days 13 and 14): hello-devops answers on an EC2 instance, and your cleanup script removes it.
- Ansible (Part 9): the second run of your playbook reports no changes.
- Service mesh (Part 15): you can measure a canary split through Envoy or a mesh.

"The dashboard looks fine" is not a check. A good acceptance check has three properties:
- It is observable: it looks at the running system, not at your memory of setting it up.
- It is binary: anyone who runs it gets PASS or FAIL, with no judgment call.
- It is runnable: one command, so you can repeat it after every change.

Compare two versions of stage 7. Weak: "Argo CD works." Strong: "After a merge, with no kubectl, `kubectl -n argocd get application hello-devops` reports Synced and Healthy." The weak version cannot clearly fail, so passing it tells you nothing.

The lab's `security/capstone-check.sh` turns 11 of the 14 stages into such checks. Each prints PASS, FAIL or SKIP. SKIP means a tool or address is missing, for example cosign not installed. The script ends with a count and exits with 1 if anything failed, so the same file could run in CI later.

Run it after every stage, and read every line, not only the one for the stage you just finished. Adding a later stage often breaks an earlier one: a new policy that rejects Redis, or a port-forward that grabbed port 8081. An older line that turns red points you straight at the cause. You run the whole test suite for the same reason, not only the newest test.

sections.h: Break it on purpose: a game day
sections.body:
A game day is a planned session where you break things on purpose and watch how the system, and you, respond. So far you have only seen hello-devops working, which tells you little about what happens when Redis dies. Before each drill, write down what you expect to see. Afterwards, write down what happened. Wherever the two differ, your picture of the system was wrong, and that is what you write up.

Five drills, each testing a different part of the course:
1. Deploy an image tagged `:latest` through git. Expect Kyverno to reject it and Argo CD to show the sync error.
2. Delete one hello-devops Pod. Expect the Deployment to replace it and the dashboard to show only a blip.
3. Scale Redis to 0. Expect `/readyz` to return 503, the Pods to go unready, an alert to fire, error logs in Kibana and a failed span in Jaeger.
4. Change the Deployment by hand with `kubectl edit`. Expect Argo CD's self-heal to put git's version back.
5. Release a version that fails its readiness probe. Expect the rollout to stall, then fix it with `git revert` alone.

If you only have time for one, do drill 3. A single fault shows up in metrics, logs and traces at once, which is why you built all three.

For each drill, write a short runbook: how you noticed, what you checked, what fixed it. Then write one blameless postmortem (Day 49) for the drill that surprised you most. Interviewers like these, because they show how you think when something is broken.

sections.body:
Your repository is now your portfolio, so give it a README that an engineer can read in five minutes:
1. What it is, in two sentences.
2. An architecture diagram, like the one in this lesson.
3. How to run it: one command per stage, in order.
4. What the pipeline proves: tests, a scan, an SBOM, a keyless signature and SLSA Build L2 provenance.
5. Two or three decisions with their trade-offs, for example Kyverno over Gatekeeper, or kind over a cloud cluster.
6. What you would do next with more time.

Spend the most time on point 5. Write each decision as a short architecture decision record (ADR): the situation, the options, what you chose and what it costs. Anyone can follow a tutorial to install a tool. Your reasons for choosing it, and what you gave up, are what show judgment.

Then record a five-minute demo. Make a one-line change, open a pull request, merge it, and show the new version in `curl`, on the dashboard, in Kibana and in a trace. Five minutes is enough to show the whole loop and short enough that people watch it.

For interviews, turn your game day into stories. Describe what broke, what you saw first, what you checked and what fixed it. A story about a Redis outage in your own cluster tells an interviewer more than a list of 20 tools on a CV.

A certification gives your learning a shape and a deadline, and some job filters look for one. Your capstone shows what you can actually do. You want both, and the capstone is good exam practice.

The CNCF publishes the official curriculum for each of its exams on [GitHub](https://github.com/cncf/curriculum), with the weight of each domain:
- KCNA (Kubernetes and Cloud Native Associate): the beginner-friendly one. Kubernetes fundamentals 44%, orchestration 28%, app delivery 16%, architecture 12%.
- CKAD (Application Developer): app design and build, deployment, observability, config and security, networking. The best fit for a developer.
- CKA (Administrator): troubleshooting is the biggest domain at 30%, which is Day 46 and your game day.
- CKS (Security Specialist): supply chain security is 20%, which is Part 17.
- Newer exams match later parts: PCA (Prometheus), OTCA (OpenTelemetry), ICA (Istio), CBA (Backstage), KCA (Kyverno), CNPA (platform engineering).

The CKA and CKAD curricula follow Kubernetes v1.37 now. Third-party guides, not the Linux Foundation pages, describe KCNA as multiple choice and CKA, CKAD and CKS as hands-on tasks in a terminal. Check formats and prices on the Linux Foundation's exam pages before you book; discounts are frequent.

Two other vendors publish their facts openly. HashiCorp's [Terraform Associate (004)](https://developer.hashicorp.com/certifications/terraform-associate) is multiple choice, one hour, online proctored, US$70.50 plus local taxes, and valid for two years. GitHub offers certifications for Foundations, Actions, Advanced Security, Administration and Copilot. AWS and Red Hat (whose RHCE exam is built on Ansible) run their own programs; check their pages for the current list.

sections.body:
At your current pace of 30 to 45 minutes a day, this is the plan I would follow:
1. Weeks 1 to 4, Kubernetes depth. Work through the CKAD curriculum on your kind cluster, one domain a week. Redo the Day 46 break-and-fix lab without notes. Book the exam if a date helps you.
2. Weeks 5 to 8, one real cloud. Start from your Day 13 account and deploy hello-devops to one managed Kubernetes service with Terraform (Part 8), OIDC from GitHub Actions, and a budget alert. Destroy it at the end of every session.
3. Weeks 9 to 12, one specialty. Choose observability (SLOs, PCA or OTCA), platform engineering (a Backstage template, CNPA) or security (KCSA, then CKS after CKA).

Every week, whatever the stage:
- Read one chapter of [Google's SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/), free online.
- Ship one small change to a real project, your capstone or a work repository.
- Write down one thing you learned, in your own words. That note is the cheapest retrieval practice there is.

At work, look for places where this course meets your Kotlin and Gradle day job, for example:
- A Gradle build cache in CI.
- A signed JVM image.
- A team label on a service.
- An alert on an SLO.

Ship one of those for your team before you install another tool on your laptop.

lessons.analogy: The capstone is your driving test after months of lessons in an empty car park. Each lesson taught one skill alone, such as steering, mirrors or parking. The test puts them all on a real road at once, with traffic, and the examiner ticks specific boxes on a sheet. Yours is kinder than a real test: you can run `capstone-check.sh` as often as you like, and failing it costs nothing.

steps.say: Take stage 2: the image reports its version and runs as non-root. Start the container from the 1.2.0 image and ask it.
steps.code:
$ docker run -d --name capstone -p 8000:8000 hello-devops:1.2.0
$ curl -s localhost:8000/ | jq
{
  "host": "738841dd8ef1",
  "message": "Hello, DevOps!",
  "version": "1.2.0",
  "visits": 1
}

steps.say: Check the user without trusting your memory of the Dockerfile. `--entrypoint id` replaces gunicorn with the `id` command, inside the same image.
Look ahead to stage 8 while you are here. This is the counter Prometheus will scrape, so if it is missing now, no dashboard can fix it later.
Now make one of these binary. This `if` prints PASS or FAIL, and it is the pattern every line of `capstone-check.sh` follows.
steps.code:
$ got=$(curl -s localhost:8000/ | jq -r .version)
$ if [[ "$got" == "1.2.0" ]]; then echo "PASS  app reports 1.2.0"; else echo "FAIL  app reports '$got'"; fi
PASS  app reports 1.2.0

steps.say: Run the whole script at this early point, with the app address set to the container. Almost everything fails, which is normal this early. Read the output as your to-do list, in order.
steps.code:
$ APP_URL=http://localhost:8000/ GITHUB_USER=you VERSION=1.2.0 security/capstone-check.sh
FAIL  Deployment hello-devops is not ready (kubectl -n hello get pods)
PASS  App at http://localhost:8000/ reports version 1.2.0
FAIL  Argo CD Application hello-devops not found in namespace argocd
SKIP  cosign not installed (brew install cosign)
FAIL  Prometheus at http://localhost:9090 has no hello_requests_total (is the port-forward running?)
FAIL  Jaeger at http://localhost:16686 has no services yet (send some requests first)
1 passed, 8 failed, 2 skipped

steps.say: That run is trimmed to six of the eleven lines; the others fail the same way, because kind is not running yet. Work down the list, run the script after each stage, and commit whenever a line turns green. Stop the container with `docker rm -f capstone`.

code.title: security/capstone-check.sh
code.src:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Capstone acceptance checks (Day 68).
# Each check runs one command and prints PASS, FAIL or SKIP.
# SKIP means "the tool or endpoint is not there", for example Dynatrace or a stopped stack.
# The script exits with 1 when any check fails, so it also works in CI.
#
# Needs: curl, jq, kubectl (pointing at your kind cluster). Optional: gh, cosign.
# Usage:   GITHUB_USER=<you> VERSION=1.2.0 security/capstone-check.sh
# Override any address, for example: PROM_URL=http://localhost:9091 security/capstone-check.sh
set -uo pipefail

GITHUB_USER="${GITHUB_USER:?set GITHUB_USER to your GitHub user name}"
VERSION="${VERSION:?set VERSION to the release you deployed, for example 1.2.0}"
APP_URL="${APP_URL:-http://localhost:8081/}"
PROM_URL="${PROM_URL:-http://localhost:9090}"
GRAFANA_URL="${GRAFANA_URL:-http://localhost:3000}"
ES_URL="${ES_URL:-http://localhost:9200}"
JAEGER_URL="${JAEGER_URL:-http://localhost:16686}"
JVM_REPO="${JVM_REPO:-${GITHUB_USER}/hello-jvm}"
owner=$(echo "$GITHUB_USER" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')

pass=0 fail=0 skip=0
ok()   { echo "PASS  $1"; pass=$((pass + 1)); }
bad()  { echo "FAIL  $1"; fail=$((fail + 1)); }
miss() { echo "SKIP  $1"; skip=$((skip + 1)); }

# 1. Kubernetes (Part 10): the Deployment is fully rolled out.
if kubectl -n hello rollout status deploy/hello-devops --timeout=60s > /dev/null 2>&1; then
  ok "Deployment hello-devops is rolled out"
else
  bad "Deployment hello-devops is not ready (kubectl -n hello get pods)"
fi

# 2. The app answers through the kind NodePort and reports the released version.
got=$(curl -fs --max-time 5 "$APP_URL" | jq -r .version 2>/dev/null)
if [[ "$got" == "$VERSION" ]]; then ok "App at $APP_URL reports version $VERSION"
else bad "App at $APP_URL reports version '${got:-no answer}', expected $VERSION"; fi

# 3. Parts 6 and 17: every app Pod runs the released GHCR image, never :latest.
images=$(kubectl -n hello get pods -l app=hello-devops -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.containers[*].image}' 2>/dev/null)
want="ghcr.io/${owner}/hello-devops"
if [[ -n "$images" ]] && ! tr ' ' '\n' <<< "$images" | grep -v -q "^${want}[:@]" \
  && ! grep -q ':latest' <<< "$images"; then
  ok "Pods run ${want} (not :latest)"
else
  bad "Pods run '${images:-nothing}', expected ${want}:<version> or @sha256:..."
fi

# 4. Part 11: Argo CD reports the app Synced and Healthy.
st=$(kubectl -n argocd get application hello-devops -o jsonpath='{.status.sync.status}/{.status.health.status}' 2>/dev/null)
if [[ "$st" == "Synced/Healthy" ]]; then ok "Argo CD: Synced/Healthy"
elif [[ -z "$st" ]]; then bad "Argo CD Application hello-devops not found in namespace argocd"
else bad "Argo CD: $st"; fi

# 5. Part 17: the cluster refuses a :latest image (Kyverno disallow-latest-tag).
# --dry-run=server sends the request through admission, but stores nothing.
out=$(kubectl -n hello run capstone-latest --image=nginx:latest --restart=Never --dry-run=server 2>&1)
if grep -q 'created' <<< "$out"; then bad "A :latest Pod was accepted. Is Kyverno installed and policy/ applied?"
elif grep -qi 'latest' <<< "$out"; then ok "Kyverno rejects :latest"
else bad "Could not ask the cluster: $(tail -n 1 <<< "$out")"; fi

# 6. Part 17: the image is signed by your release workflow (needs cosign).
if command -v cosign > /dev/null; then
  if cosign verify "${want}:${VERSION}" \
    --certificate-identity "https://github.com/${GITHUB_USER}/hello-devops/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v${VERSION}" \
    --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com > /dev/null 2>&1; then
    ok "cosign: ${want}:${VERSION} is signed by release.yml"
  else bad "cosign could not verify ${want}:${VERSION}"; fi
else miss "cosign not installed (brew install cosign)"; fi

# 7. Part 7: the last hello-jvm CI run succeeded (needs gh).
if command -v gh > /dev/null; then
  c=$(gh run list --repo "$JVM_REPO" --limit 1 --json conclusion -q '.[0].conclusion' 2>/dev/null)
  if [[ "$c" == "success" ]]; then ok "hello-jvm: last CI run succeeded"
  elif [[ -z "$c" ]]; then miss "no CI runs found in $JVM_REPO (set JVM_REPO=owner/repo)"
  else bad "hello-jvm: last CI run is '$c'"; fi
else miss "gh not installed"; fi

# 8. Part 12: Prometheus has the app's request counter.
n=$(curl -fsG --max-time 5 "${PROM_URL}/api/v1/query" --data-urlencode 'query=sum(hello_requests_total)' \
  | jq -r '.data.result[0].value[1] // empty' 2>/dev/null)
if [[ -n "$n" ]]; then ok "Prometheus: sum(hello_requests_total) = $n"
else bad "Prometheus at $PROM_URL has no hello_requests_total (is the port-forward running?)"; fi

# 9. Part 13: Grafana is up and its database is fine.
g=$(curl -fs --max-time 5 "${GRAFANA_URL}/api/health" | jq -r .database 2>/dev/null)
if [[ "$g" == "ok" ]]; then ok "Grafana is healthy"
else bad "Grafana at $GRAFANA_URL did not answer /api/health"; fi

# 10. Part 14: Elasticsearch holds log documents.
docs=$(curl -fs --max-time 5 "${ES_URL}/_count" | jq -r '.count // 0' 2>/dev/null)
if [[ "${docs:-0}" -gt 0 ]]; then ok "Elasticsearch holds $docs documents"
else bad "Elasticsearch at $ES_URL has no documents (is Fluent Bit shipping?)"; fi

# 11. Part 14: Jaeger has received traces from at least one service (Jaeger's v3 HTTP API).
svc=$(curl -fs --max-time 5 "${JAEGER_URL}/api/v3/services" | jq -r '.services // [] | join(", ")' 2>/dev/null)
if [[ -n "$svc" ]]; then ok "Jaeger has traces from: $svc"
else bad "Jaeger at $JAEGER_URL has no services yet (send some requests first)"; fi

echo
echo "${pass} passed, ${fail} failed, ${skip} skipped"
[[ "$fail" -eq 0 ]]

commands.what: Run all capstone acceptance checks and print PASS, FAIL or SKIP for each.
Print the user ID the image runs as. Expect 10001, not 0.
Ask the app on kind which version it runs.
Wait until the rollout is complete, or fail after 60 seconds.
Print Argo CD's sync and health status, for example Synced/Healthy.
Send a :latest Pod through admission without creating it. Kyverno should reject it.
Ask Prometheus for the total request count.
List the services Jaeger has received traces from.
Count the documents (log lines) stored in Elasticsearch.
Show the result of the last hello-jvm CI run.
Game day drill: take Redis away and watch every signal react.
Undo the last commit with a new commit; Argo CD rolls the cluster back.

lessons.mistake: Building all 14 stages first and testing at the end leaves you with five broken things at once, and you cannot tell which one causes the others. Finish one stage, make its check pass, commit, and only then start the next.
lessons.real_world: A new platform engineer's first project can look a lot like this capstone. They take one service from commit to production on the golden path, with every check green, and present it to the team. The team learns where the path is rough, and the new engineer learns the whole system in two weeks instead of six months.

task.title: Run your capstone end to end
steps: Copy the 14-stage checklist into a `CAPSTONE.md` in your repository, one line per stage, each with its acceptance check.
Work through stages 1 to 7 in order. Run `security/capstone-check.sh` after each stage, and commit when its lines pass.
Add stages 8 to 11. Start the port-forwards or Compose stacks so the endpoints answer on ports 9090, 3000, 9200 and 16686.
Do stages 13 and 14. Leave stage 12, Dynatrace, for last, or skip it.
Run a game day with at least three of the five drills. Write what you expect first, then what happened, then a runbook for each.
Write the README: what it is, a diagram, how to run it, what the pipeline proves, two decisions with trade-offs, and what comes next.
Record a five-minute demo: a one-line change goes from pull request to production, and you show it in curl, on the dashboard, in Kibana and in a trace.
hints: Fix stages in order. One red early stage often explains several red later ones.
If a check fails because of an address, override it with an environment variable, for example `PROM_URL=http://localhost:9091`.
A laptop has limits. Run the observability tools either in Compose or in the cluster, not both at once.
task.done_when: `security/capstone-check.sh` ends with `0 failed`, your README explains the system, and your demo shows one change from commit to dashboard.

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences the path of one code change through your capstone, from git push to a user, and how you know at each step that it worked. Mention CI, the registry, Argo CD and observability.
explain_back.answer: A pull request runs CI, which lints and tests the code and must be green before merge; a version tag then runs the release workflow. The release scans the image, pushes it to GHCR, writes an SBOM and signs it, and I verify that with `verify-release.sh`. A commit that changes the image tag in git tells Argo CD what to run. I know the deploy worked when Argo CD shows Synced and Healthy and the rollout completes. Then Prometheus and Grafana show traffic and errors, Kibana shows the logs and Jaeger shows traces, so I can see that users actually get the new version.

recap: The capstone sends one change through every part of the course, with hello-devops and hello-jvm.
A stage is done when its runnable, binary acceptance check passes, not when it looks fine.
capstone-check.sh runs 11 checks; rerun it after every stage, because new stages break old ones.
A game day with written expectations turns broken things into runbooks and interview stories.
Present with a README, a diagram, decisions with trade-offs and a five-minute demo.
Pick certifications from the official curricula, check prices on the owner's site, and keep shipping.

check.q: Your capstone check shows FAIL for Argo CD (OutOfSync) and FAIL for Prometheus. What do you fix first?
options: Prometheus, since metrics come first
Argo CD, since the deploy feeds the rest
Both at once, in two terminals
Neither: rerun until they pass
check.why: Stages depend on earlier ones: if the app is not deployed, Prometheus has nothing to scrape.

check.q: Which is the best acceptance check for stage 7, GitOps?
options: Synced/Healthy after a merge, with no kubectl
Argo CD is installed and looks fine
The team agrees that GitOps works
The Argo CD web page loads in a browser
check.why: It looks at the running system, gives pass or fail, and tests the actual promise of GitOps.

check.q: You build apps at work and want a Kubernetes certification about running your own apps. Which curriculum fits best?
options: KCNA: broad, beginner-friendly basics
CKS: securing clusters and supply chains
CKAD: designing, deploying and configuring apps
CKA: running clusters, 30% troubleshooting
check.why: The CKAD curriculum is built around application design, deployment, configuration and observability.

interview.q: Walk me through a project that shows your DevOps skills.
interview.a: I built a small Python service and a Kotlin service and took them end to end. Pull requests run CI; a tag builds a multi-arch image that is scanned, signed with cosign and attested; Argo CD deploys it to Kubernetes from git. Prometheus, Grafana, an EFK stack and Jaeger observe it, and Kyverno and RBAC guard the cluster. Every stage has an acceptance check in one script, and I ran game days, for example taking Redis down and following the failure through metrics, logs and traces.

interview.q: How do you know a deployment actually worked?
interview.a: I check in layers. First the rollout completes and the readiness probes pass, and in GitOps Argo CD shows Synced and Healthy. Then a smoke test calls the service and checks the version it reports. Then the user-facing signals: error rate and latency against the SLO in Prometheus and Grafana, plus logs and traces for anything odd. If those move the wrong way, I roll back with git revert before I start debugging.

interview.q: Which certification would you take next, and why?
interview.a: I would start with the CKAD, because I come from application development and its curriculum is about designing, deploying and configuring apps on Kubernetes. Then the CKA, because troubleshooting is its biggest domain at 30%, and that is the skill that matters most on call. I would check the format and price on the Linux Foundation's page before booking. In parallel I would keep the capstone running, because the exam and the project practise the same skills.

deeper.body:
The hardest capstone test I know is to delete the cluster and rebuild it from git.

Everything you deploy now lives in files: the kind config, Helm values, Kyverno policies, the Argo CD Application, the ExternalSecret. In theory that means `kind delete cluster` loses nothing that matters. In practice, most first attempts fail, because some step only ever happened by hand. Maybe you installed Kyverno from your shell history, or labelled the namespace with `kubectl label` and never wrote it down. Every one of those steps is a gap in your disaster recovery.

Try it like this:
1. Write a `bootstrap.sh` that creates the kind cluster, installs Argo CD, and applies one Argo CD Application.
2. Let Argo CD install everything else from git: Kyverno, External Secrets Operator, kube-prometheus-stack, Fluent Bit and the app. The [app-of-apps pattern](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/cluster-bootstrapping/) from Day 48 is made for this.
3. Time it: run `kind delete cluster --name devops`, start a stopwatch, run the bootstrap script, and stop when `security/capstone-check.sh` shows 0 failed.
4. Every time the rebuild needs a manual step, move that step into git and run the test again.

Two things usually go wrong. Order matters: Kyverno's policies need Kyverno's CRDs first, and the app needs its namespace labels before Pod Security can judge it. Argo CD sync waves (Day 48) solve this, by giving each Application a number and syncing low numbers first. And state outside git does not come back: the Redis counter, Prometheus history and Elasticsearch logs are gone. That is fine for a lab, and it is the reason real teams keep data in managed services or back it up separately.

When the rebuild is one command and the check is green, write the time in your README. In an interview, "the whole platform rebuilds from git in N minutes" covers GitOps, infrastructure as code and disaster recovery in one sentence.

sources.title: CNCF curriculum for all CNCF exams

recap: Platform engineering turns repeated DevOps work into self-service golden paths, run as a product for developers.
Backstage is a framework for developer portals; the platform is the templates, pipelines and clusters behind it.
The CNCF maturity model scores five aspects on four levels; pick your next step instead of aiming for level 4 everywhere.
FinOps loops through inform, optimize and operate, and starts with an owner label on every cost.
Showback comes first: each team sees its own cost, and idle cost gets its own line.
A golden path ships its guardrails: pinned actions, signed images, narrow RBAC, policies and owner labels.
The capstone runs one change through the tools of every part, with a runnable check for each stage.
Game days, runbooks, a clear README and a short demo turn the capstone into a portfolio.
Choose certifications from the official curricula: CKAD suits a developer, and CKA gives troubleshooting 30%.

flashcards.front: What is an internal developer platform?
flashcards.back: The self-service capabilities a platform team offers, such as templates, pipelines, environments and dashboards.
A supported, ready-made way to do a common task, made easier than doing it alone.

flashcards.front: Is a golden path the only allowed path?
flashcards.back: No. Teams may leave it with a reason, and many teams leaving tells you the path is wrong.
An open source framework for developer portals: software catalog, templates, TechDocs and plugins.

flashcards.front: What are the five aspects of the CNCF platform maturity model?
flashcards.back: Investment, adoption, interfaces, operations and measurement.

flashcards.front: Adoption by mandate vs adoption by choice: which maturity levels?
flashcards.back: Pushed by mandate is level 2. Pulled by teams who want it is level 3.

flashcards.front: What are the three FinOps phases?
flashcards.back: Inform, optimize and operate, repeated as a loop.
Allocation: give every cost an owner, with tags in the cloud and labels in Kubernetes.

flashcards.front: Why do Kubernetes requests drive cost?
flashcards.back: The scheduler reserves what a Pod requests, whether it uses it or not.

flashcards.front: Showback or chargeback: what is the difference?
flashcards.back: Showback reports each team's cost while the money stays central; chargeback moves the cost into each team's budget.

flashcards.front: What is idle cost in a Kubernetes cluster?
flashcards.back: What you pay for node capacity that no workload requested.

flashcards.front: Why track cost per request instead of the total bill?
flashcards.back: Totals grow with the business; cost per request shows whether each unit of work got cheaper.
Which team owns the service in the developer portal: the same idea as the team label on its Pods.
It creates a new repository with a copy of a template repository's files and a fresh history.

flashcards.front: What makes a good acceptance check?
flashcards.back: It is observable, binary (pass or fail) and runnable with one command.
A planned session where you break things on purpose and compare what happens with what you expected.

flashcards.front: Which domain carries the most weight in the CKA curriculum?
What does HashiCorp publish about the Terraform Associate (004) exam?
flashcards.back: Multiple choice, one hour, online proctored, US$70.50 plus taxes, valid for two years.

quiz.q: Which sign shows that a platform has reached "intrinsic pull" adoption?
options: A manager made it mandatory for all teams
Teams choose it because it is faster
It has more plugins than it had last year
The platform team has grown to 20 people
quiz.why: In the CNCF model, pull means teams adopt the platform because it helps them, not because they were told to.

quiz.q: A platform team ships a Backstage portal with no templates or self-service behind it. What have they built?
options: A complete internal developer platform
A replacement for their CI system
A FinOps cost reporting tool
A front door with little behind it
quiz.why: Backstage is a framework for the portal; the value is in the capabilities it exposes.

quiz.q: A team's Pods request 4 CPUs in total but use 0.5 on average. Which FinOps lever fits first?
options: Right-size the requests from real usage
Buy reserved capacity for all 4 CPUs
Move the workload to another cloud
Add more nodes to be on the safe side
quiz.why: Requests reserve capacity whether used or not, so matching them to real use frees the most for the least effort.

quiz.q: You create payments-api from the hello-devops template and rename it with sed. `helm lint` now fails: there is no Chart.yaml in chart/payments-api. What did the rename miss?
options: The Helm repository's URL
The image tag in values.yaml
The team label on the Pods
The chart folder's own name
quiz.why: sed changes file contents, not folder names, so the chart folder still has the old name; the template's instructions must say so.

quiz.q: Finance wants every team to see its cluster cost each month, but budgets stay central for now. Which practice is that?
options: Showback
Chargeback
Reserved capacity
Spot pricing
quiz.why: Showback reports cost per team without moving money between budgets; chargeback would move it.

quiz.q: Which of these is a binary, runnable acceptance check for the capstone?
options: The dashboard looks healthy today
The team feels the deploy went well
kubectl rollout status passes within 60s
Argo CD was installed last week
quiz.why: It looks at the running system, takes one command, and returns pass or fail.

quiz.q: On game day you scale Redis to 0. Where do you expect the first visible sign in hello-devops?
options: The image signature stops verifying
/readyz returns 503 and Pods go unready
Argo CD deletes the Deployment
Kyverno rejects the running Pods
quiz.why: The readiness endpoint returns 503 when Redis is set but down, so Kubernetes stops sending traffic to those Pods.

quiz.q: You want to prove Kubernetes security skills, including supply chain security. Which exam's curriculum has a Supply Chain Security domain at 20%?
options: KCNA
CKAD
CKS
PCA
quiz.why: The CKS curriculum lists Supply Chain Security at 20%, next to cluster and system hardening.

quiz.q: A bad release was synced automatically by Argo CD with self-heal on. How do you roll back?
options: kubectl rollout undo, then wait
Delete the Argo CD Application
git revert the change and push
Restart the Argo CD server Pod
quiz.why: Git is the source of truth; a hand rollback would be undone by self-heal, while a revert commit is synced like any change.

quiz.q: Prometheus on kind has no hello_requests_total at all. What is the most likely cause?
options: The ServiceMonitor does not match the Service
Grafana's data source uses the wrong colours
The app image is signed with cosign
Kyverno is running in Audit mode
quiz.why: Prometheus only scrapes what a ServiceMonitor selects, so a label mismatch means no target and no series.
